recipe.history:
Burrata — Italian for 'buttered' — was invented in the early twentieth century in Puglia, the heel of Italy's boot, as a practical solution to a common problem. Cheesemakers at the Bianchini farm near Andria, around 1920, found themselves with excess scraps and curds left over from the production of fresh mozzarella. Rather than discard them, they wrapped these soft inner stracciatella curds — shredded mozzarella soaked in fresh cream — inside a thin, smooth outer pouch of fresh mozzarella. The result was a cheese of extraordinary luxury: an unassuming white ball that, when cut or torn open, released a flowing interior of cream-soaked curds, rich and voluptuous and tasting purely of fresh milk. Burrata spread slowly through southern Italy before the rest of the world caught on. It requires fresh whole milk, skill, and speed — burrata should be eaten the same day it is made — which limited its reach until modern refrigeration and air freight brought it to tables worldwide.

Burrata arrived on American restaurant menus in the early 2000s, initially appearing on upscale Italian-American antipasto boards alongside heirloom tomatoes and basil. Its migration to burgers happened swiftly once chefs grasped the logic: a burger needs a fat-rich, meltable element, and burrata provides that in the most extravagant possible way. Unlike sliced mozzarella, which can turn rubbery under heat, torn burrata placed on a just-rested patty flows and spreads naturally, enveloping the beef in its creamy stracciatella interior. The contrast of the warm, caramelized beef crust against the cold, silky cheese became one of the signature moments of the new-American burger renaissance. By the 2010s, burrata burgers were appearing on menus from Brooklyn to Los Angeles.

The first time I tore a ball of burrata over a burger was at a backyard party where someone had brought over too much cheese from a fancy grocery trip and not enough ideas for what to do with it. We had patties on the grill, we had this beautiful, room-temperature ball of burrata sitting in its little container, and someone just went for it. They tore it directly over the just-pulled patty and we all watched the cream pour out and mingle with the beef juices. Nobody said anything for a full thirty seconds after the first bite. It is that kind of cheese.

To cook a burger to anything other than medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit at the center — when you are serving it with burrata is to fundamentally misunderstand the dish. The cheese is cold or at most room temperature, rich with cream, delicate and yielding. It needs a patty that is warm and juicy enough to slightly warm it on contact, to mingle its juices with the cream, to provide a savory, mineral contrast to the cheese's purity. A well-done patty is a dry platform. A medium-rare patty is a partner. The beef must be pink, the crust must be deep brown, and the whole assembly must be constructed and eaten quickly, before the burrata finishes warming and the contrast is lost.
ingredients: 4 oz fresh burrata (1 large ball or 2 small), at room temperature
Good-quality extra-virgin olive oil for drizzling
instructions: 1. Make the ciabatta-style buns: This dough is very wet and slack — do not be tempted to add more flour. Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm water; bloom 10 minutes. Combine with flour, milk, olive oil, and salt. Mix with a dough hook on medium-low 10 minutes; the dough will be very sticky and stretchy.
2. Transfer to an oiled bowl. Perform 3 sets of stretch-and-fold every 30 minutes. Cover and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours) for best flavor.

3. Turn cold dough onto a well-floured surface. Gently shape into a rough rectangle without deflating. Cut into 4 equal squares or rectangles. Transfer to a floured parchment-lined baking sheet; proof at room temperature 1.5–2 hours until puffy.

4. Preheat oven to 450°F (230°C) with a cast-iron pan on the bottom rack. Dust buns with flour. When oven is ready, add 1 cup water to the bottom pan to create steam and immediately slide buns in. Bake 18–22 minutes until golden and hollow when tapped. Cool fully before slicing.

5. Roast the cherry tomatoes: Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Toss cherry tomatoes with olive oil, garlic, thyme, salt, and red pepper flakes. Spread on a baking sheet in a single layer. Roast 25–30 minutes until blistered and beginning to collapse. Cool slightly.

6. Make the basil oil: Blanch basil leaves in boiling salted water 10 seconds; immediately transfer to an ice bath. Squeeze dry. Blend with olive oil and salt on high until smooth and bright green. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve if desired. Set aside.
7. Take the burrata out of the refrigerator 30 minutes before serving so it reaches room temperature.

8. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties slightly wider than the buns. Press a center dimple. Season generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder on both sides.
9. Heat a cast-iron skillet over very high heat until smoking. Add olive oil.

10. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes until a deep, dark crust forms. Flip once. Cook 2–3 more minutes until an instant-read thermometer inserted in the center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C). Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes — do not top with cheese yet.
11. Toast split ciabatta buns cut-side down in the skillet fat 60–90 seconds.
12. Assemble: Drizzle basil oil over the bottom bun. Add arugula leaves and a spoonful of roasted cherry tomatoes.
13. Place the rested patty on top. Immediately tear the burrata into large, irregular pieces and arrange over the hot patty, letting the creamy interior spill over the surface.
14. Season the burrata with flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper. Drizzle with a thread of extra-virgin olive oil and a few drops of aged balsamic.
15. Crown with the top bun and serve at once — the burrata will continue to warm and the dish peaks within 60 seconds of assembly.
